## Introduction  {.unnumbered}

In this problem set, you will consider a wide variety of tools for 
_classification_. In addition to comparing different classifiers, you will also
examine the _calibration_ of different predictions, see how post-processing 
techniques can be used to improve calibration, and see how classifiers can be 
used to perform anti-bias audits in large data sets. 

## Data Files  {.unnumbered}

For this data set, we introduce a data taken from the 
[Federal HMDA Dataset](https://ffiec.cfpb.gov/data-browser/data/2025). Under
the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act, lenders are required to report details of 
all mortgage applications they process to the federal government to ensure
compliance with the Fair Housing Act (and related rules and regulations).
I have taken the full data set of approximately 13.5 million mortgage 
applications and focused on a smaller set of around 2.3 million applications for
which all data was clean and easily interpreted. The reduced data set can
be found [here](./data/ps03_hdma.csv.gz). 

Most of the features of this data set are self-explanatory: 

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(readr)
hdma_data <- read_csv("https://michael-weylandt.com/STAT3106/problem_sets/data/ps03_hdma.csv.gz")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
library(readr)
hdma_data <- read_csv("./problem_sets/data/ps03_hdma.csv.gz")
```

```{r}
library(skimr)
skim(hdma_data)
```

Note that three features in this data set refer to protected classes under 
US antidiscrimination law (race, sex, and ethnicity, here reported as 
"Hispanic/Latino" or "Not Hispanic/Latino" following relevant [Federal
Guidance](https://www.census.gov/topics/population/hispanic-origin/about.html).)
You should not use these 'sensitive' features in your initial analysis until you
reach the anti-discrimination study in the final question. 

The `tract` quantities return to the census tract in which the property to be
purchased is located. `ltv` refers to `loan-to-value`, the fraction of the 
property's total value to be paid *via* the mortgage.[^ltv] 

The (binary) response of interest is the `approved` flag, indicating whether
the application was ultimately approved. This data is reasonably well-balanced
with approximately 66% approvals and 33% disapprovals.

[^ltv]: If I am buying an $800,000 property and putting a conventional 20% down.
I will pay \$160,000 up front and take out a mortgage on the remaining \$640,000,
yielding a 80% loan to value. 

## Review: ML Foundations and Regression (12 points) {#q1}

Answer the following short answer questions, worth two points each: 

1. When fitting a model via a first-order (stochastic gradient) methods, 
   the choice of *(mini-)batch size* is an important parameter; machine learners
   typically choose the mini-batch size to balance the pros and cons of 
   full batch and one-at-a-time (online) gradient methods. 
   
   Explain these pros and cons and why a moderate mini-batch size is typically
   used (32, 128, 512, *etc*). 
   
   You do not need to argue for a specific amount, as the optimal batch size is
   often model, data, and hardware specific. Just explain what the pros and cons
   of each extreme end of the spectrum are.
   
2. Rank the following models from highest to lowest (statistical) complexity:

   - Ridge Regression
   - OLS
   - $3$-Nearest Neighbor Regression
   - 4th Order Polynomial Regression (fourth order expansions across all 
     combinations of features)
   - A spline model with 4 knots in one feature and no non-linearity in any other
     features
   - $n-2$-Nearest Neighbor Regression
   
3. What are the practical trade-offs when deciding the proportion of data to 
   allocate to the validation set versus the training set in a data-scarce 
   environment? How does cross-validation attempt to navigate these tradeoffs?
4. *(Multi-)collinearity* is an oft-cited boogeyman when applying regression
   models. Explain why this is not actually a problem if you are only interested
   in prediction and what sort of techniques can be used to mitigate any adverse
   effects. 
5. To predict the number of rare birds observed in a given region, enterprising
   ornithologists will build a model that incorporates weather, time of year,
   migration patterns, food availability, and proximity to humans. What type
   of *generalized linear model* would be appropriate for this task? Note 
   both the link function and the sampling distribution? 
6. LASSO regression and Additive Models both attempt to provide a high degree
   of *interpretability*. Compare and contrast these two methods, taking care to
   specifically contrast the *type of interpretability* each method provides
   and the different regimes in which they may be used. 

## Practice of Machine Learning (12 points) {#q2}

Consider the scenario below in which I describe a hypothetical application of
ML. There are (at least) 4 issues in how the ML system is developed, tested, 
and deployed. Identify **three** distinct issues and, for each issue you identify,
describe: 

- The mistake that was made (1 points)
- The likely adverse impact arising from the mistake (1 points)
- What should have been done instead (2 points)

(This is what lawyers might call an "Issue Spotter" question.)

**Scenario**: Following your helpful feedback in [Problem Set #02](./ps02.qmd#q1),
the good folks at Hamilton, Butler and Low (HBL) Consulting have decided to 
rework their automated talent interview pipeline. The People Analytics team
were asked to develop a (probabilistic) talent recruitment classifier that can
be used to perform resume scans; the result was Project CROWN (Candidate Ranking
for Onboarding and Welcoming Newcomers). 

CROWN's objective was to predict whether an applicant represents an 
"Elite Associate" ($Y = 1$), defined as finishing in the top 5% of their cohort 
across billable impact and annual reviews. Training on 4,000 historical applicant
files from 2018 to 2023 (yielding exactly 200 positive and 3,800 negative cases),
the engineers extracted hundreds of resume keywords (tokens), problem-solving 
scores, and behavior records from things like participation in sponsored recruiting
events and alumni network recommendations. Because partner interview slots were 
strictly limited, the HBL management committee established a simple decision 
rule: any candidate whose predicted probability of eliteness (PPE) $\hat{p}$ 
exceeded 50% would automatically receive an invitation to final-round interviews
with firm leadership, while those below 50% would be rejected without further 
review.

The CROWN team initially benchmarked linear classifiers before moving to 
considering tree-based methods and ensembles. When fitting a Support Vector 
Machine (SVM) the model achieved a 95.0% accuracy with minimal tuning. Eager to 
extend this already highly performant model to capture non-linear credential 
combinations, the team transitioned to `xgboost`. They fit the boosted tree
ensemble with a max tree depth of 12, a high learning rate of $0.99$, 
and disabled all row and column sub-sampling to make sure all features were
well captured by the model. After running the algorithm for 3000 rounds, 
`xgboost` had an in-sample cross-entropy (logistic loss) of 0.001% and
a cross-validated AUC of 93%. These strong performance scores convinced the
People Analytics team that the `xgboost` predictions were accurate and 
well-calibrated and that CROWN was ready to go live for the upcoming recruiting
season.

## Calibration (9 points) {#q5}

When building a (binary) classifier, the property of _calibration_ ensures
that the model's predicted (output) probabilities match the actual
probabilities. (You can think of this as a 'holistic' accuracy measure for
probabilistic classifiers that looks at all points on the curve, not just
at a single point defining the decision boundary.)

For a model to be calibrated, we want $\P(Y | X) = \hat{p}(X)$ for all
possible inputs $X$. While easily stated, this is not actually quite so 
simple to check in practice. We need 'repeated' $X$ to get a good estimate
of the real probabilities $\P(Y|X)$ and outside of designed scenarios, exact
replicates in $X$ are hard to find. 

This motivates the use of a _binning_ strategy: we find several points
where $\hat{p}(X)$ is around 10% and hope that 10% of the true labels for 
those points are positive. Let's see this in action for our simple penguin
sex model:

```{r}
library(broom)
penguins_ece <- penguins |> 
    mutate(is_female = (sex == "female")) |> 
    glm(is_female ~ body_mass + flipper_len, 
        data=_, 
        family=binomial) |>
    augment(type.predict="response") |>
    mutate(bucket=ntile(.fitted, n=10)) |>
    group_by(bucket) |>
    summarize(bucket_mean_model=mean(.fitted), 
              bucket_mean_label=mean(is_female), 
              bucket_min_model=min(.fitted), 
              bucket_max_model=max(.fitted),
              bucket_error=bucket_mean_model - bucket_mean_label,
              n=n()) |>
    mutate(ece = weighted.mean(abs(bucket_error), n))
```

yielding

```{r}
#| echo: false
library(gt)
library(glue)
penguins_ece |>
  gt(id="tbl_penguins_ece") |>
    cols_hide(c(ece)) |>
    fmt_percent(c(starts_with("bucket_"))) |>
    tab_style(
        style=cell_text(color="#aa0000"), 
        locations=cells_body(
            columns=bucket_error,
            rows=bucket_error < 0)) |>
    cols_merge(c(bucket_min_model, bucket_max_model), 
               pattern="[{1}-{2}]") |>
    cols_label(bucket="Bucket Number", 
               bucket_error="Calibration Error",
               bucket_min_model="Range of Predicted Probabilities",
               bucket_mean_model="Average Predicted Probability",
               bucket_mean_label="True Fraction", 
               n="Number of Observations") |>
    tab_header("Calibration Analysis of Penguins 2 Factor Sex-Prediction Model", 
               glue("Expected Calibration Error {scales::percent(first(penguins_ece$ece), accuracy=0.01)}"))
```

This is decent - particularly in some parts of the model - but in other parts
of the curve our probabilities may be off by 15% or more. Taking the (bin-size
weighted) average of the bucket-wise calibration errors, we get a measure
called *Expected Calibration Error* (ECE), which is around 
`r scales::percent(mean(penguins_ece$ece), accuracy=0.01)` for this particular
set of forecasts.[^in_sample] [^l1]

[^in_sample]: Properly, it's best to assess ECE on out-of-sample (test) 
predictions, but I'm being a bit sloppy here to simplify exposition. 

[^l1]: Note that ECE as defined here is the $\ell_1$ (taxicab / Manhattan) norm
of the calibration errors for each bucket. $\ell_2$ (root mean squared calibration
error) and $\ell_{\infty}$ (maximum calibration error) versions exist and work
essentially the same way. 

ECE is a good measure, but it is a bit unstable in practice. Selecting different
numbers of buckets or even just 'shifting' the bucket endpoints around can change
your results, sometimes quite dramatically. Despite this, we'll use it as our
primary metric for this question. 

Here, seeing that calibration isn't all that great (we're off by 8% on average)
we might want to _adjust_ our model to improve calibration. One approach is to
consider a different family of models: alternatively we can take the output
of the model we already have and _post-process_ it to improve calibration. 
In situations where the probabilities are too low (red) we might want to 'bump'
them up a bit and where they are too high (black) we might want to similarly 
adjust them downwards. 

Naively, we might do this by pushing probabilities for the 'true' outcomes
all the way to 1 and to 0 for the 'false' outcomes, but this essentially destroys
the shape of our predictor and functionally reduces us to fitting $1$-nearest
neighbors. A better approach is to adjust probabilities *while maintaining
ordering*: so if we have two observations, with $\hat{p} = (0.3, 0.4)$, we
could post proces to $(0.2, 0.4)$ or $(0.4, 0.5)$ or maybe even $(0.45, 0.45)$,
but not to $(0.4, 0.2)$ because we'd break the existing ordering. This sounds
like it might be hard, but thankfully there's a classical statistical technique
called *isotonic regression* that does exactly this. 

The details of isotonic regression are beyond this course, but the below image
should get the main idea across: 

```{r}
#| echo: false
penguins |> 
    drop_na() |> 
    select(flipper_len, body_mass) |> 
    arrange(flipper_len) |> 
    mutate(iso_body_mass = isoreg(flipper_len, body_mass)$yf) |> 
    ggplot(aes(x=flipper_len)) + 
    geom_point(aes(y=body_mass)) + 
    geom_line(aes(y=iso_body_mass), color="red4", lwd=2) + 
    theme_bw() + 
    xlab("Flipper Length") + 
    ylab("Body Mass") + 
    ggtitle("Isotonic Prediction of Body Mass from Flipper Length")
```

Here, the isotonic regression curve (red) minimizes the MSE to the observed
values (black dots) among all *non-decreasing* curves. 

(Make sure you understand why this is exactly the type of constraint we might
want to apply when post-processing a set of predictions to improve calibration.)

If we apply this to our penguin model from above, we could get the following
*post-processed* predictions. 

```{r}
penguins_logistic_iso <- penguins |> 
    mutate(is_female = (sex == "female")) |> 
    glm(is_female ~ body_mass + flipper_len, 
        data=_, 
        family=binomial) |>
    augment(type.predict="response") |>
    arrange(.fitted) |> 
    mutate(.fitted.iso = isoreg(.fitted, is_female)$yf, 
           sex=if_else(is_female, "Female", "Male")) 
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
penguins_logistic_iso |>
    slice_sample(n=20) |>
    arrange(.fitted) |>
    select(sex, body_mass, flipper_len, .fitted, .fitted.iso) |>
    gt(id="tbl_penguins_iso") |>
    fmt_percent(starts_with(".fitted"), 
                decimals=2) |>
    cols_label(body_mass="Body Mass (g)", 
               flipper_len="Flipper Len (mm)", 
               sex="Sex",
               .fitted="Logistic Regression Prediction",
               .fitted.iso="Isotonically Recalibrated Logistic Prediction")
```

These recalibrated predictions no longer have the linear structure of logistic
regression, but they exhibit far better calibration: 

```{r}
#| echo: false
penguins_ece_iso <- penguins_logistic_iso |> 
    mutate(bucket=ntile(.fitted.iso, n=10)) |>
    group_by(bucket) |>
    summarize(bucket_mean_model=mean(.fitted.iso), 
              bucket_mean_label=mean(is_female), 
              bucket_min_model=min(.fitted), 
              bucket_max_model=max(.fitted),
              bucket_error=bucket_mean_model - bucket_mean_label,
              n=n()) |>
    mutate(ece = weighted.mean(abs(bucket_error), n))

penguins_ece_iso |>
  gt(id="tbl_penguins_ece_iso") |>
    cols_hide(c(ece)) |>
    fmt_percent(c(starts_with("bucket_"))) |>
    tab_style(
        style=cell_text(color="#aa0000"), 
        locations=cells_body(
            columns=bucket_error,
            rows=bucket_error < 0)) |>
    cols_merge(c(bucket_min_model, bucket_max_model), 
               pattern="[{1}-{2}]") |>
    cols_label(bucket="Bucket Number", 
               bucket_error="Calibration Error",
               bucket_min_model="Range of Predicted Probabilities",
               bucket_mean_model="Average Predicted Probability",
               bucket_mean_label="True Fraction", 
               n="Number of Observations") |>
    tab_header("Calibration Analysis of Penguins 2 Factor Sex-Prediction Model After Isotonic Recalibration", 
               glue("Expected Calibration Error {scales::percent(first(penguins_ece_iso$ece), accuracy=0.01)}"))
```

**As shown, overfitting is a serious danger of this workflow. When doing this
properly, you should make sure to train your model on one split, recalibrate
on another, and compute test calibration on a third.**

## Comparing Regression & Classification on the Same Task (12 points) {#q6}

In this question, we will take another look at the 
[California drought prediction task](./data/ps02_ca_drought.csv) introduced in
the previous problem set. 

You originally considered this as a *regression* task in which
you were attempting to predict the drought severity score. We're now going to 
instead consider the *classification* task of determining simply whether we are
in a drought or not. 

Re-download the CA drought data and create a new response variable indicating
when the PDSI is below 2 (moderate drought or worse). 

Fit classification models to this data set, including (at a minimum): 

- Ridge-Regularized Logistic Regression
- Lasso-Regularized Logistic Regression
- $K$-Nearest Neighbors Classification
- A simple tree-based classifier
- Random forest classifier
- `xgboost` classifier

Observe best practices (cross-validation and similar) for hyperparameter tuning 
and estimating test performance. Which of these has the best performance and why?
(Make sure to omit the original PDSI variable from these models and use only the
SST variables; the PDSI variable is clearly 'too good' a predictor.)

Next, repeat your analysis using the _regression_ versions of each method on 
the original data set. Compare your results to the classification versions. 

- On which task do you achieve better performance?
- How would you compare regression and classification performance measures? 
- Is the 'shape' of the predictions the same across all 10 models? (*I.e.*,
  even if the values differ, do they consistently identify the same 'high' and
  'low' years?)
- For models that allow you to calculate feature importance measures, are the
  same features important?
  
When comparing 'paired' classification and regression tasks (like those
considered here), there are two countervailing forces: 

- Regression provides more information per observation 
- Classification limits the amount by which one can be wrong (0/1), so the task
  is fundamentally 'easier' in some sense. 
  
In general, it is hard to say which effect will win out for a particular problem.
Which effect seems to have been stronger in this comparison? Justify your answer. 

## Fairness in Machine Learning (9 points) {#q7}

In many situations, when applying a classifier as an automated decision rule, 
there are important *non-discrimination* laws that must be followed.[^regr] In
this question, we're going to *audit* the HDMA data for signs of discrimination.
As we will see, there are *many* different mathematical formalisms for bias and
they do not always (or even often!) agree. 

### Demographic Parity (4 points)

The simplest measure of bias in classification is known as *(deviation from) 
demographic parity*. Demographic parity is the idea that the percentage of
'positives' from each sub-population should match the percentage of
that sub-population in the broader population: *e.g.*, if a state has a 
population that is 30% African-American, its elected officials should be
(approximately) 30% African-American as well.[^baseline_pop]
For our population, we're going to use the total population of mortgage 
applicants as the reference population: so if female mortgage applicants are
30% of all applicants, they should also hold (approximately) 30% of all 
_approved_ mortgages. 

Examine the HDMA data. Do you see any signs that demographic parity is 
systematically violated by any bank against any groups? 

Note that this is a rather unrealistic analysis. Other fairness measures such
as _equality of opportunity_ would likely be more appropriate here, but we don't
have actual repayment records for this data so this would not be feasible for us
to calculate. 

[^baseline_pop]: Selecting the _right_ baseline population to compare against
is a bit tricky: when looking at, *e.g.*, the composition of a corporate board,
should it reflect America as a whole, American adults, American adults over
the age of 50 (plausible 'senior executives'), the shareholders of that 
corporation, the customer population of the business, *etc*?


### An Audit Construction (5 points)

One way to _audit_ this type of data for signs of bias is to via a carefully
constructed `LOCO` analysis. Specifically: we would like to consider two models: 

$$f_1: \text{Race} \approx f(\text{Features Other Than Approval})$$

and 

$$f_2: \text{Race} \approx f(\text{All Features})$$

If $f_2$ is signifcantly more accurate than $f_1$ -- *i.e.*, if knowing the
approval status helps to predict the applicant's race more than just knowing
their baseline economic info -- that is evidence that there may be a systematic
racial difference in approval rates.[^condition]

Use a powerful classifier of your choosing[^rf] to conduct this type of audit
study on the sensitive attributes of race, sex, and Hispanic/Latino ethnicity.
(This should be 3 distinct studies. You don't need to consider any sort of
'intersectionality' for this problem unless you want to go deeper.)

[^condition]: The `LOCO` behavior is important here. We want to compare 
"Everything" *vs.* "Everything except Race". It is not enough to simply see 
if Race is predictive of approval rates, because that may be a (permissible)
indirect relationship. If, due to historical biases, one group has systematically
lower incomes, banks may approval their applications at a lower rates due to
the (permissible) lower incomes and higher chance of payment issues, not
racial bias. Not surprisingly, this is a rather contentious topic: in essence, 
we are asking whethere disperate outcomes are *per se* evidence of bias. While
many arguments can be made on both sides, this construct of 'impact over and
above just economics' is my current best understanding of the law and will
suffice for this problem.



See <https://fairmlbook.org/> for *much* more on this topic. 

[^regr]: Non-discrimination laws apply to 'regression-type' systems as well, but
the mathematical formalisms for fairness in regression are not nearly as well
developed.

[^rf]: I default to Random Forests for things like this, but the 'cool kids' 
might reach for `xgboost`.
